The Pastoral Epistles
PAS-tur-uhl ih-PISS-uhlz
noun (canon)
From pastoral (Latin pastor, shepherd) and epistle (Greek epistole, a letter sent); so named because they instruct Christ's shepherds in ordering His church.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Pastoral Epistles are the three letters of Paul to two pastors — First and Second Timothy and Titus — in which the apostle instructs his sons in the faith on church order, qualified men, and sound doctrine. They open with Paul's own name and apostolic claim: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour" (1 Tim 1:1); "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God" (2 Tim 1:1); "Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ" (Titus 1:1). Here Christ gives the church her standing manual for appointing elders and deacons, setting the qualifications, charging the public reading and preaching of the word, and guarding the deposit of truth against false teachers. The critical academy advances the theory that these letters are pseudonymous — forged in Paul's name by a later hand — pointing to vocabulary and church structure. This dictionary rejects that theory as both unproven and corrosive: a forged letter that says "I Paul" (compare 2 Tim 1:1) is a lie, and the Spirit does not inspire lies. The early church received all three as Pauline, and the internal claims, personal greetings, and travel notices are the marks of genuine apostolic correspondence. This dictionary confesses these three letters as the inspired, Pauline, and authoritative charter of the pastoral office.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The three New Testament letters of Paul to Timothy and Titus, instructing pastors in church order, qualified officers, and sound doctrine. Their Pauline authorship is affirmed against the critical theory that they were forged under his name.

expand to see more

THE PASTORAL EPISTLES, noun. The three Pauline letters to Timothy and Titus on the ordering of the church.

They comprise First Timothy, Second Timothy, and Titus, each opening with Paul's name and apostolic claim.

"Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour" (1 Tim 1:1).

They supply the qualifications of elders and deacons, the charge to preach, and the guard of sound doctrine.

Their genuine Pauline authorship is confessed against the academy's theory of pseudonymous forgery.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Tim 1:1 — "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ, which is our hope;"

2 Tim 1:1 — "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus,"

Titus 1:1 — "Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness;"

2 Tim 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The chief assault on these letters is the historical-critical theory of pseudonymity, which holds them to be later forgeries falsely signed with Paul's name — a theory this dictionary rejects as unproven and as making the Spirit the author of a lie.

expand to see more

The academy teaches that the Pastorals are pseudonymous: written after Paul's death by an admirer who borrowed his name, alleging that their vocabulary, their settled church offices, and their warnings against error point to a later age. The argument fails on its own terms. Word-counts across three short personal letters prove nothing about authorship; elders and deacons appear already in Acts and Philippians within Paul's lifetime; and false teaching was present from the first. More gravely, the theory cannot be squared with inspiration. A letter that declares "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ" (2 Tim 1:1) and sends personal greetings is either true or a forgery; there is no innocent ancient convention that turns "I Paul" into honest fiction when the Holy Ghost is the author.

The early church knew the difference between genuine and spurious writings and received these three as Paul's without dispute, while rejecting actual forgeries. To grant the critical theory is to surrender 2 Timothy 3:16 in the very letter that asserts it. The recovery is plain confession: these are the words of the apostle Paul, breathed out by God, and therefore the binding charter for ordering Christ's church in every age.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name joins pastoral, of the shepherd, with epistle, a sent letter, marking these as Paul's shepherding correspondence to his fellow shepherds.

expand to see more

Epistle, from Greek epistole, a letter dispatched to a person or church.

Pastoral, from Latin pastor, shepherd, because the letters equip shepherds of the flock.

The title is a later convenience; the letters themselves name only their author, Paul, and their recipients.

Timothy was Paul's "own son in the faith" (1 Tim 1:2); Titus, "mine own son after the common faith" (Titus 1:4).

The contested word pseudonymous means falsely-named — precisely the charge this dictionary denies.

Usage

"He preached through the Pastoral Epistles to teach the young congregation how Christ would have His church ordered."

"The Pastoral Epistles give the elder his qualifications and the church her marching orders for sound doctrine."

"We affirm the Pastoral Epistles as genuinely Pauline, against every theory of later forgery."
